source_text: Scimus ex dominico praecepto, quod caro infirma sit, spiritus promptus. Non ergo nobis blandiamur, quia Dominus consensit carnem infirmam esse. Propterea enim praedixit spiritum promptum, ut ostenderet, quid cui debeat esse subjectum, scilicet, ut caro serviat spiritui, infirmior fortiori, ut ab eo etiam ipsam fortitudinem assumat. Colloquatur spiritus cum carne de communi salute, nec jam de incommodis carceris, sed ipso agone et praelio cogitans. Timebit forsitan caro gladium gravem, et crucem excelsam, et rabiem bestiarum, et summam ignium poenam, et omne carnificis ingenium in tormentis. Sed spiritus contra ponat sibi et carni, acerba licet ista, a multis tamen aequo animo excepta, imo et ultro appetita, famae et gloriae caussa; nec a viris tantum, sed etiam a foeminis, ut vos quoque, benedictae, sexui vestro respondeatis. Longum est, si enumerem singulos, qui se gladio confecerint, animo suo ducti. De foeminis ad manum est Lucretia, quae vim stupri passa, cultrum sibi adegit in conspectu propinquorum, ut gloriam castitati suae pareret, Mutius, manum suam dexteram in ara cremavit, ut hoc factum ejus fama haberet. Minus fecerunt philosophi: Heraclitus, qui se bubulo stercore oblitum exussit; item Empedocles, qui in ignes Aetnaei montis dissilivit; et Peregrinus, qui non olim se rogo immisit: cum foeminae quoque contempserint ignes: Dido, ne post virum dilectissimum nubere cogeretur; item quum Asdrubalis uxor, quae jam ardente Carthagine maritum suum supplicem Scipionis videret, cum filiis suis in incendium patriae devolavit. Regulus, dux Romanorum, captus a Carthaginiensibus, cum se unum pro multis captivis Carthaginiensibus compensari noluisset, maluit hostibus reddi et in arcae genus stipatus undique extrinsecus clavis transfixus, tot cruces sensit. Bestias foemina libens appetiit, et utique aspides, serpentes tauro vel urso horridiores, quas Cleopatra immisit sibi, ne in manus inimici perveniret. Sed mortis metus non tantus est, quantus tormentorum. Itaque, cessit carnifici meretrix atheniensis? quae conscia conjurationis, cum propterea torqueretur a tyranno, et non prodidit conjuratos, et novissime linguam suam comestam in faciem tyranni exspuit, ut nihil agere se scirent tormenta, etsi ultra perseverarent. Nam quod hodie apud Lacedaemonas solemnitas maxima est, διαμαστίγωσις, id est, flagellatio, non latet. In quo sacro, ante aram nobiles quique adolescentes, flagellis affliguntur, astantibus parentibus et propinquis, et uti perseverent adhortantibus. Ornamentum enim et gloria deputabitur majore quidem titulo, si anima potius cesserit plagis, quam corpus. Igitur, si tantum terrenae gloriae licet de corporis et animi vigore, ut gladium, ignem, crucem bestias, tormenta contemnant, sub praemio laudis humanae, possum dicere, modicae sunt istae passiones ad consecutionem gloriae coelestis et divinae mercedis. Si tanti vitrum? quanti margaritum? Quis ergo non libentissime tantum pro vero habeat erogare, quantum alii pro falso?
pass_a_gloss: We know from the Lord's command that the flesh is weak, the spirit is willing. Therefore, we should not flatter ourselves because the Lord has agreed that the flesh is weak. For this reason, He predicted a willing spirit, so that He might show what the flesh owes to be subject to, namely, that the flesh serves the spirit, the weaker to the stronger, so that it may also assume strength from it. The spirit converses with the flesh about common salvation, and now not about the discomforts of prison, but thinking about the very struggle and battle. Perhaps the flesh will fear the heavy sword, and the high cross, and the rage of beasts, and the greatest punishment of fires, and every ingenious torture of the executioner. But the spirit sets against itself and the flesh, although these things are bitter, nevertheless, they have been endured by many with an equal mind, and even sought out voluntarily, for the sake of fame and glory; and not only by men, but also by women, so that you too, blessed ones, may respond to your sex. It is long to enumerate individuals who have killed themselves with the sword, led by their own mind. Among women, Lucretia is at hand, who, having suffered the force of rape, drove a knife into herself in the sight of her relatives, so that she might obtain glory for her chastity. Mucius burned his right hand on the altar, so that this deed of his might have fame. Philosophers have done less: Heraclitus, who covered himself with cow dung and burned himself; likewise Empedocles, who leaped into the fires of Mount Aetna; and Peregrinus, who not long ago threw himself on a pyre: since women have also despised fires: Dido, lest she be forced to marry after her beloved husband; likewise when Asdrubal's wife, who saw her husband supplicant to Scipio as Carthage was burning, threw herself into the fire of her native land with her children. Regulus, a Roman general, captured by the Carthaginians, when he did not want to be exchanged for many Carthaginian captives, preferred to be returned to the enemies and, enclosed in a kind of chest, transfixed all over with nails, suffered so many crosses. A woman willingly sought out beasts, and especially asps, serpents more dreadful than a bull or a bear, which Cleopatra inserted into herself, so that she might not fall into the hands of the enemy. But the fear of death is not as great as the fear of torments. And so, did the Athenian prostitute yield to the executioner? Who, conscious of a conspiracy, when she was being tortured by a tyrant for this reason, and did not betray the conspirators, and finally spat out her own tongue, which she had chewed, into the face of the tyrant, so that they might know that torments could do nothing to her, even if they persevered further. For what is today the greatest solemnity among the Lacedaemonians, διαμαστίγωσις, that is, flagellation, is not hidden. In this sacred ritual, noble adolescents are afflicted with whips before the altar, with their parents and relatives standing by and encouraging them to persevere. For it will be considered an ornament and glory, with a greater title, if the soul yields to the blows rather than the body. Therefore, if such earthly glory is allowed from the strength of body and soul, so that they despise the sword, fire, cross, beasts, torments, under the reward of human praise, I can say that these sufferings are moderate for the attainment of heavenly glory and divine reward. If so much is given for glass? How much for a pearl? Who, therefore, would not willingly spend as much for the truth as others do for falsehood?
pass_b_english: We know from the Lord's own teaching that the flesh is weak while the spirit is willing. So let's not coddle ourselves just because the Lord has admitted the flesh's frailty. He highlighted the spirit's eagerness precisely to show what the flesh owes its superior: the weaker must serve the stronger, drawing strength from that service. The spirit needs to talk to the flesh about their shared salvation—not about the discomforts of prison anymore, but about the actual contest and battle ahead. The flesh may well flinch at the heavy sword, the high cross, the savagery of beasts, the ultimate penalty of fire, and every diabolical device the executioner can invent. But the spirit must confront both itself and the flesh with a different ledger: bitter as these torments are, countless people have endured them with equanimity, even sought them out voluntarily, all for the sake of fame and glory—and not just men, but women too, so that you, blessed ones, can answer the call of your own sex.

It would take too long to list every individual who fell on their own sword at their mind's prompting. Among women, Lucretia stands ready: raped, she drove a dagger into herself before her kinsmen's eyes to win glory for her chastity. Mucius Scaevola burned his right hand on the altar so his deed would win renown. The philosophers did less: Heraclitus smeared himself with cow dung and burned himself alive; Empedocles threw himself into the fires of Mount Etna; and Peregrinus, not long ago, leaped onto a pyre. Women have despised fire as well: Dido, rather than be forced to remarry after her beloved husband's death; and the wife of Hasdrubal, watching her husband beg Scipio for mercy as Carthage burned, hurled herself and her children into the flames of her homeland. Regulus, a Roman general captured by the Carthaginians, refused to be exchanged for many Carthaginian prisoners; he chose to be handed back to the enemy, shut in a kind of chest, and pierced all over with nails from the outside—suffering, in effect, countless crosses. A woman eagerly courted the beasts, and specifically asps—serpents more dreadful than bull or bear—which Cleopatra applied to herself rather than fall into enemy hands. Yet the fear of death is nothing compared to the fear of torture. So did an Athenian prostitute break under the executioner? She knew of a conspiracy; when the tyrant tortured her for it, she never betrayed the conspirators, and at the end she chewed off her own tongue and spat it in the tyrant's face, proving that torments could do nothing to her even if they continued. We all know the Lacedaemonians' greatest solemnity today, the διαμαστίγωσις—that is, flagellation. In this sacred rite, noble youths are whipped before the altar while their parents and relatives watch and urge them to endure. It counts as a higher honor and glory if the soul yields to the blows before the body does. Therefore, if mere earthly glory can draw such strength from body and soul that they despise sword, fire, cross, beasts, and torture for the reward of human praise, I can say these sufferings are moderate indeed for gaining heavenly glory and a divine reward. If people pay so much for glass, what will they pay for a pearl? Who, then, would not gladly spend as much for the truth as others spend for a lie?

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the complex historical examples (Lucretia, Mucius, philosophers, Dido, Asdrubal's wife, Regulus, Cleopatra, and the Athenian prostitute) and the theological distinction between the flesh and the spirit. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent, accurate rendering that preserves all agency, modality, and doctrinal distinctions. The Greek term διαμαστίγωσις is correctly identified and translated. Scripture-alluded concepts (the flesh being weak/spirit willing) are handled correctly.
